problem: The generic code is shown without its type parameter list: 'function identity(x: T): T { return x; }' and 'class Box { constructor(public value: T) {} }'. As written, T is never declared, so neither snippet is valid TypeScript and the compiler would report 'Cannot find name T'. A student copying this gets a broken example of the very feature being taught.
fix: Write the type parameters: function identity<T>(x: T): T { return x; } and class Box<T> { constructor(public value: T) {} }. Then say: the angle brackets declare T as a type parameter, and it is filled in at each call, e.g. identity<number>(5) or, inferred, identity(5).

where: Section 2, annotations paragraph, and Quiz Q6 answer
problem: 'number[] or Array for an array of numbers' and 'Array of numbers: number[] or Array.' both drop the type argument. Bare 'Array' means Array<any>, which is not the same as an array of numbers, so the statement as printed is wrong and the quiz answer is incomplete.
fix: Write 'number[] or Array<number> for an array of numbers' in Section 2, and in Q6 answer 'Array of numbers: number[] or Array<number>'. Add that the version in angle brackets is the generic form and the two are equivalent for this type.

where: Worked example 1, [code] block and output lines
problem: The example is about TypeScript, but the code shown is Python-style pseudocode (a = 2, print, len(str(...))) and it contains a stray 'print(7)'. The output lines 5, 2, 7 come from that pseudocode, not from the TypeScript in the question, and nothing in the question corresponds to the third line. A student cannot map the code or the output to parts (a), (b), (c).
fix: Replace the code block with the TypeScript under discussion: function add(a: number, b: number): number { return a + b; } const u: User = { id: 7, name: 'Ravi' }; and show the compiler messages instead of print output, e.g. add(2, 3) → 5 (one line of output); add('2', 3) → error TS2345, no output; { id: '7', name: 'Ravi' } → error TS2322 on id. Drop the stray line entirely so the printed output matches the three parts.

where: Section 1, second paragraph, and Worked example 1 step 2
problem: 'A mismatch stops the build, so the browser never sees the broken file' and 'tsc reports an error and stops. No JavaScript runs' are too strong. By default tsc still writes app.js when there are type errors; it only refuses to emit when noEmitOnError is true (or when a build tool is configured to fail).
fix: Say: tsc reports the error and exits with a non-zero status; with noEmitOnError set in tsconfig.json it also skips writing app.js. For an exam answer, 'the call fails to compile — it is a type error' is what matters.

problem: 'then removes every type' / 'Every annotation, interface and type alias is erased' is not true for enums, which Section 3 itself introduces. A non-const enum compiles to a real JavaScript object that exists at run time, which is why Size.Small works in the browser.
fix: Add one sentence: interfaces, type aliases and annotations leave no run-time trace, but an enum does — it becomes an ordinary JavaScript object, so Size.Small is available at run time. (A const enum is inlined and leaves nothing.)

problem: Grouping instanceof and typeof as 'run-time checks' that an interface cannot be used with is loose. typeof is also a value-level operator and cannot take a type as an operand, so the sentence can leave a student unsure whether typeof is allowed at run time at all.
fix: Say: an interface or type alias is not a value, so it cannot appear on the right of instanceof, and you cannot write typeof SomeInterface. typeof works only on a real variable, e.g. typeof x === 'string', which is exactly how you narrow an unknown.
